title: A Wardrobe for the Language
premise: Petra Marchetti has spent twelve years writing postcards to the burned-down house on Via delle Rose, addressed to his grandmother's old name—a name the family abandoned after a scandal no one will speak of. When her funeral draws a stranger who greets the mourners by that forbidden surname, Petra realizes someone outside the family still remembers who they were before they erased themselves. Following the stranger back to the village where the fire happened, Petra uncovers the truth: his grandmother chose exile to protect a love she could never claim, and the demolition of the ruined house is scheduled in six weeks. In the end, Petra claims the letters as his own inheritance, saves the house's facade from destruction by having it declared a memorial, and finally writes one postcard signed with both names—his and hers.
about_author: Ulyana Zhou is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undeliverable mail in a northern port city. Their fiction explores how families survive their own silences, and this is their second novel.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. We meet him at the post office counter, mailing postcard number four hundred and thirty-eight to an address that no longer exists, then returning to the flat above his late grandmother's tailor shop. The chapter establishes his ritual of almost-saying: every card ends mid-sentence. Emotional beat: tender, controlled loneliness—the reader senses he's writing to more than a house.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. At Nonna Lucia's funeral, amid the correct condolences, a weathered stranger named Teo kisses the coffin and says 'Addio, signora Vassallo'—a surname Petra has never heard spoken aloud. His aunt Rosa goes white and hustles everyone out. Emotional beat: a crack in twelve years of careful silence; Petra's invisibility suddenly feels like a cage rather than a shelter.

chapters.title: What Rosa Burned
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, with a flashback to childhood. He confronts Rosa, who admits only that the family changed its name after 'the fire' and forbids him to look for Teo. That night he finds a locked tin box in the shop's false drawer containing one unmailed letter, dated the week of the fire. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into resolve; duty versus curiosity begins its war.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Bar
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo, sixty and dying slowly of something he doesn't name, drinks alone and remembers Lucia Vassallo as the woman who hid him during the worst year of his life. He knows Petra has been asking about him. Emotional beat: guarded tenderness; Teo recognizes in Petra the same hunger to be unnamed—and the same refusal to stay hidden.

chapters.title: Via delle Rose
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Against Rosa's orders, Petra travels to the village and finds the burned house—half-ruin, half-shrine, scheduled for demolition in five weeks. Teo is there, tending the garden no one planted. He recognizes the handwriting on Petra's postcards, which have been arriving for years, forwarded by the postmistress. Emotional beat: two keepers of the same secret finally standing in the place it was made.

chapters.title: The Year of the Fire
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, told through Teo's account and the tin-box letter. Lucia, married and respectable, loved a woman named Serafina; when the village found out, the house was set alight, Serafina vanished, and Lucia buried her name to protect her infant daughter—Petra's mother. Emotional beat: grief reframed as devotion; Petra understands his family's silence was armor, not shame.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Rosa arrives in the village to drag Petra home and finds him living in the ruin with Teo, restoring the garden. She reveals her own wound: she burned Lucia's letters after the funeral decades ago out of fear, and has regretted it ever since. Emotional beat: confrontation softening into confession; the found-family triangle forms against the ticking clock of the bulldozers.

chapters.title: Everything I Almost Said
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra reads all twelve years of his own postcards aloud to Teo in the gutted kitchen, finishing every sentence he once abandoned—including the ones about his mother, his shame, his hope. Teo answers with what Lucia said to him the night of the fire. Emotional beat: the climax of speech; saying it, at last, out loud, in the room where saying it cost everything.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Petra petitions the town council to stop the demolition, presenting the letters as evidence the house is a site of memory. Rosa testifies publicly under the name Vassallo, reclaiming it before the whole village. The council grants a compromise: the facade and garden become a protected memorial. Emotional beat: public reclamation; private history becomes shared ground.

chapters.title: Signed, Both Names
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, epilogue-like. One year later, the shop bears two signs, the garden blooms, and Teo—frailer but content—teaches Petra Serafina's recipes. Petra mails a final postcard to Via delle Rose, now deliverable, signed 'Petra Marchetti Vassallo.' Emotional beat: quiet resolution; identity as something chosen, inherited, and finally spoken.
